The research shows no significant difference in weight loss between intermittent fasting and daily calorie restriction in most cases — with a notable recent exception.

When total calories are matched between the two approaches, intermittent fasting produces nearly identical weight loss to continuous daily calorie restriction. A major 2026 Cochrane review examined 22 randomized controlled trials with nearly 2,000 participants and found the weight loss difference between the two methods was "statistically indistinguishable from zero." [1] A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 studies reached the same conclusion: intermittent fasting is not superior to calorie restriction for weight loss when calories are equal.  [2]

A 2025 study published in Annals of Internal Medicine found that a 4:3 intermittent fasting approach (eating freely 4 days per week, restricting calories heavily on 3 days) produced greater weight loss than daily calorie restriction: 7.6% average weight loss versus 5% in the continuous restriction group.  [3]

The researchers designed both groups to have identical weekly calorie deficits (34%), yet the 4:3 pattern still outperformed.  [3]

The Cochrane review noted that current evidence provides little information about whether one method is easier to maintain than the other. Some people find intermittent fasting psychologically easier because they don't count calories daily, while others experience higher hunger levels during fasting windows.  [2]

When weight loss does occur with either method, both approaches show similar improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar control. The 4:3 intermittent fasting study did show slightly more favorable changes in these cardiometabolic markers, though researchers noted these were secondary outcomes requiring larger studies for confirmation.  [3]
